explanation: Cassava, also called manioc or yuca, is native to South America. Bubble tea, with its tapioca pearls, first became popular in Taiwan in the 1980s.

claims.text: Tapioca is starch extracted from the cassava root.
Tapioca is not starch from sago palm, taro or rice.
Cassava, also called manioc or yuca, is native to South America.
Bubble tea with tapioca pearls first became popular in Taiwan in the 1980s.

writerNotes: Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3). Lint: content:check run on the batch until this item showed no errors. Rival test: Sago pearls look the same and are sometimes made from tapioca, so sago tempts; but tapioca by definition is cassava starch. Taro is used in other bubble tea toppings. Against the key: none. Volatility: evergreen; no time words, and nothing depends on knowledge newer than mid-2026. Regional: bubble tea is sold on every continent, and cassava is a staple across Africa, Asia and Latin America. Style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens, single quotation marks, explanation of 25 words. Myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches any claim. Mystery and encore checks: not applicable to a practice item. Seed: 4: many players know tapioca without knowing its plant. Doubts: none on the key. Which Taiwanese tea shop invented bubble tea is disputed, so c4 says only where and when it became popular.

Tapioca does not come from sago palm, taro or rice (true sago is a different starch).
Cassava (manioc, yuca) is native to South America.
Pearl milk tea (bubble tea) caught on in Taiwan in the 1980s, with tea shops in Taichung and Tainan credited.

evidence.restatement: Tapioca is starch from the cassava root.
Tapioca is not made from sago palm, taro or rice, although sago pearls look similar.
Cassava, also called manioc or yuca, is native to South America.
Bubble tea with tapioca pearls was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s and first caught on there in the late 1980s.

claimResults.note: 'First became popular' holds only for the first local hits; sources usually say 'originated in the 1980s' and describe the boom in the 1990s. High-risk: counts only with external evidence in the other check (section 9.9).

issues.note: 'First became popular in Taiwan in the 1980s' is safest as 'was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s'; the boom came in the 1990s.
